blk_part_01_part_1_kolsch_a_beer_with_ru.text: Kölsch is a pale, clear and light beer from Cologne. It is top-fermented, which means the yeast works at warmer temperatures. That method gives the beer a fresh, slightly fruity taste. Brewing has a long history in the city, and Cologne's brewers' guild dates back to 1396.

blk_part_01_part_1_kolsch_a_beer_with_ru.text: The drinking customs are just as important. Kölsch comes in a narrow 0.2-litre glass called a Stange. The waiter is called a Köbes, and he carries the glasses in a round tray called a Kranz. When your glass is empty, the Köbes usually replaces it without asking. He also marks each beer on your beer mat. To stop, you put the beer mat on top of your glass. Famous brewery pubs in the Old Town include Früh, founded in 1904, and Päffgen, founded in 1883.

"Alt" refers to the old way of brewing, with top-fermenting yeast, the same basic method used for Kölsch. The result is very different, though. Altbier is dark copper or brown, with a stronger malt flavour and more bitterness.

The heart of this culture is the Old Town, which locals call "the longest bar in the world" because it has so many pubs close together. Traditional brewery pubs there include Schumacher (1838), Füchschen (1848) and Uerige (1862). Each one brews its own Altbier.

Locals often joke that you should never order Kölsch in Düsseldorf or Altbier in Cologne. Mostly, this is humour, not real hostility.
